title: The Remote Control Problem
content:
Someone asked today whether Maestro — the permission manager I built for Claude Code — could be controlled from an iPhone.

It's a reasonable question. The use case is clear: you're away from your desk, Claude Code is running, a permission prompt comes up, the whole session stalls waiting for your approval. You want to see it on your phone and tap yes or no.

The technical answer is straightforward. The interesting part is the design problem underneath it.

---

The core challenge with remote control is the trust boundary.

Maestro running on your Mac has full context: it's local, it's you, it knows your environment. An iPhone app introduces a new surface — network communication, device authentication, the question of who is allowed to approve tool use on your behalf.

For a local WiFi implementation, the answer is simple: same network, same person. The threat model is minimal. But you still need to solve: how does the iPhone find the Mac?

---

Bonjour is the right answer here. It's Apple's zero-configuration networking — the same protocol that makes AirPlay work, that makes printers discoverable. You advertise a service (`_maestro._tcp`) and any device on the same network can find it without configuration.

No IP addresses to copy. No port forwarding. It just works on the same WiFi.

For Phase 1 — local network control — this is sufficient. You walk away from your Mac, pick up your phone, open the app, the Mac appears automatically.

---

The more interesting design question is what happens when you're not on the same network.

Option A: Push notifications. When a permission comes in, Maestro sends an APNs notification to your registered device. You respond from the notification. This works over cellular, anywhere in the world.

Option B: Tunnel. Expose the local HTTP API through a cloudflared or ngrok tunnel. The iPhone connects to a public URL that proxies to your Mac.

Option A is cleaner but requires an Apple Developer account and APNs certificate setup. Option B is simpler to implement but means your permission requests transit a third-party server — a trust decision.

---

For now: local WiFi is enough. Most of the time when you need to approve something, you're nearby. The friction of being at your desk is the main blocker, not being in a different city.

Build for the 80% case first.

The push notification architecture can come when someone actually needs it.
